title: Why Whaley's name is missing from jazz books
summary: Hinton asks why Whaley, who was Duke's 'chairman of the board' and Apollo director, is omitted from books by Feather and Dance, and Whaley says he can't understand it either.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: Well, look, Tom, now, this is kind of personal. And I want to ask you how you figure this out. And I've known you and I've talked about how you help me and what an important part as we've shown here in talking, your relationship at the Apollo Theater where all the black musicians, all the jazz musicians played, all the black show people played.

Now, we talked about back in Boston, before my time, you were a kid and your recollections with Johnny Hodges and Jefferson Hilton and all the great saxophone players that came out of Boston, including Tootsie Mondello, a white saxophone player. And we've talked about your deep relationship, of the great writer of music, Duke Ellington. How close you were to him and how he trusted you to decipher his scores.
You told me how certain other musicians would do it,
would give you a score and say -- Wille Vodery, he wrote for 23 years for the Ziegfeld Follies. He'd give you a score and tell you -- he'd trust you to add two trumpets to it or two clarinets to it.

And you've told me about -- we've discussed -- and I'm aware of this and I know all this, about all of these people that you've written for, the bands that you had, you were the musical director at the Apollo Theater for years. How does it happen that in books like -- Leonard Feather's Book of Jazz, Stanley Dance 's book. Nobody mentions your name. How does that --
You know what? I can't figure that myself. See, I was chairman of the board with Duke Ellington.
Absolutely.
Duke used to tell me, tell them all, I want you to meet my chairman of the board, Tom Whaley.
Right.

And I can't understand why no one would call on me -- a guy did come from Yale and try to get me, but I was sick, and I couldn't -- he came and I was sick that week and I couldn't do the thing. But I mean other people. They know how I -- how close I was with Duke, and knew everything and even Mercer, he don't even do nothing. Mercer -- oh, I don't know what's the matter, but --
Yeah, I don't understand, but I'm

trying to figure out, Tom, -- and I'm a part of this, I'm aware of this. This is the reason I'm so glad to be a part of talking to you and putting your-- having this go into the National Archives. That people will know the importance of one black man that was through all the jazz. You're 86 years old and this is 1979.
And I can't understand how this happened. And I was in Washington in 1970, for Duke's 70th birthday party. You conducted the orchestra which I was in, and Joe Williams to sing 'For My People.'
Right.

Now, how can -- and Leonard Feather was there and many other great dignitaries was there. How is it, when I look through the discography of musicians in the '70s or farther back than that, that I don't find the name Whaley? It disturbs me greatly.
I wonder why, just like Long John Nebel, see. Sy Oliver introduced me to him, see, and he says, I ought to have you on the show sometime, but never did.

Well, I'm so happy to have you on this one and have you tell your story. I just wish -- you've been the most literate of any person I've ever interviewed. Your dates, you're the brightest, chronologically you know how to bring it about, which I'm most grateful for.
I tell you, it's no -- we set here and you're 86
years old, you set here for three and a half hours with me, straight. And you've told me all these stories and we've gone through everybody from 18-something up to 1979.

And I have some personal tapes of mine here that we just listened to where you were visiting me in 1974. And because of my deep interest in you and my love for you, I was trying to tape and find out some of the things about you then. So now I've mentioned it, and I've very disturbed and I hope that this won't happen again, that in the annals of jazz, that your name will go down in the annals of American music, a man that's so deeply associated with Duke Ellington.

And another thing. When they put that book out with all the pictures of the people in the Apollo Theater, I said, where's my picture? Why ain't my picture on there? I'm just a part -- because I was there. Ralph Cooper brought me in there, see.
Absolutely.
From the Lafayette Theater.
